items.originalTitle: Utah GOP governor on Trump and 2028: ‘It’s time for the next thing’
items.author: Lauren Fedor
items.title: Utah GOP governor on Trump and 2028: ‘It’s time for the next thing’
items.summary: Utah’s Republican governor wants his party to move beyond President Donald Trump heading into the next presidential election. “It’s time for the next thing,” Gov. Spencer Cox said in an interview on Wednesday at the POLITICO Pub, on the sidelines of the National Governors Association’s New Governors Leadership Forum in Deer Valley, Utah. Cox called on his fellow Republicans to start looking for new leadership in the wake of this month’s midterm election defeats. “This is how this works when presidents move on. We should be looking for the next leadership in our party and what that looks like,” Cox told POLITICO’s Samuel Benson. “We’ve got JD Vance and Marco Rubio, and those seem to be kind of the two choices now,” Cox said, referring to the Vice President and Secretary of State, respectively. “But I think you’ll see a lot of people step up … there are a lot of really interesting folks.” “I’m a fan of governors,” Cox added. “I think governors with executive experience are the best to lead the country.” Vance told Fox News earlier this week that he would decide “sometime next year” whether he will run for president in 2028. Rubio has dismissed suggestions that he would launch his own bid, and has said he would support Vance if the Vice President ran for the White House. “I am hopeful that there are some Republican governors that will throw their hat in,” said Cox, a two-term governor. “We can have a competition of ideas heading in to find out what's next.” Cox said that Trump still has a “really important role to play” in leading the party over the next two years, adding that the president still had an “opportunity” to strike bipartisan deals on permitting reform and other policy areas in his last two years in office. Cox called the president “unique,” adding: “He’s someone who has the attention of the country in a way that almost no president has had in my lifetime.” “People really love him or really don’t like him, but everybody’s paying attention to him,” he said.

items.originalTitle: This new early-state governor has advice for 2028 Democratic hopefuls
items.author: Alec Hernandez
items.title: This new early-state governor has advice for 2028 Democratic hopefuls
items.summary: Deb Haaland is about to take the helm of a newly-minted Democratic presidential primary battleground. She has thoughts for her party’s White House hopefuls on how to win there. Haaland, New Mexico’s incoming governor, told POLITICO that immigration will be a “top issue” in the presidential election — one that she’s “anxious” to see how future candidates plan to address — and said that engaging with rural voters in her state will be key to any successful primary campaign. “New Mexico is the fifth largest state, and we are largely rural,” Haaland told POLITICO’s Erin Doherty in an onstage interview at the National Governors Association's New Governors Leadership Forum in Utah. “There are far more rural communities than there are large cities in our state, and so this will be important for New Mexicans to to really understand or to really know that any presidential candidate understands the challenges that they're facing.” Immigration is “going to be a top issue with the 2028 presidential election,” she added. “New Mexico is an early primary state, and it happens that we're a border state, too.” Haaland’s ascension to the governor’s mansion coincides with a major change in New Mexico’s place in the Democratic Party's presidential nominating calendar pecking order. The state will now be fourth in the voting calendar behind South Carolina, Nevada and New Hampshire. The move gives New Mexicans — and their new governor — significant influence in shaping the kind of nominee the party selects to take back the White House. It’ll also pose a significant test for candidate’s engagement with Latino voters, as New Mexico ranks first nationwide in its population share of Latino residents. Some of those potential candidates have already come calling. “Rahm Emanuel was in New Mexico, and he did quite a bit of traveling around,” Haaland said, noting that several senators made their own sojourns to the state for an event hosted in October by Democratic Sen. Ben Ray Luján in Alberquerque. Former Secretary of Transportation Pete Buttigieg made his own trip to the state in September. “Whether all of them are running for president, I can't tell you, but I am really anxious to see who does.” Haaland, a former Secretary of the Interior and the first Native American woman elected to a governorship, is ready to wield her own influence in the process as well, flexing her new power broker status . “I would love to endorse, but I'll wait and see who throws their hat in the ring,” she said. Haaland was swept into office with a historic number of fellow Democrats across the country on a mandate to deliver on affordability. It’s the “biggest issue” in New Mexico, Haaland said, adding that her priority to deliver lower costs for New Mexicans will start with expanding access to affordable health care. “Right now we're talking with some of the leaders in the legislature about health care, a public option for people in New Mexico,” she said. “Health care is a top top priority.”

items.originalTitle: Bo French loses Texas country club membership
items.author: Casey He and Jonathan Martin
items.title: Bo French loses Texas country club membership
items.summary: Bo French, the far-right firebrand who centered his losing campaign for the Texas Railroad Commission on his anti-immigration stance, lost his membership at a Fort Worth country club, according to a letter obtained by POLITICO . The letter from River Crest Country Club, dated Nov. 10 and addressed to French, said the club’s board of directors voted to terminate French’s membership immediately “for reasons relating to the reputation and general welfare of the Club.” The country club, founded in 1911, is the eighth to open in the state and boasts being a “who’s who” of Fort Worth. It hosts a 6,368-yard golf course that has been a training ground for top golfers, according to its website. River Crest declined to comment, citing its policy of not doing so about “past, present and prospective members” and club operations, its general manager said in an email. French, who has a history of making controversial statements on immigration issues like the H-1B visa program, made headlines in September after going viral on social media for a post he made that appeared to disparage Asian American students at the University of Texas at Austin. His remarks capitalized on the growing anti-Indian sentiment sweeping Texas and across the nation , particularly against holders of the high-skilled worker visa, a majority of whom are from India. The post quickly drew rebukes from Democrats and some Texas Republicans, who denounced it as racist. But French stood by the post . He said he was criticizing admission and hiring policies at UT, the state’s public flagship, that he claimed discriminated against Texas residents. (State law requires a majority of admitted students at the school to be residents of the state.) French lost by 677,000 votes in his bid to sit on the influential statewide body that regulates Texas’ oil and gas industry two months later amid a statewide wipeout for the GOP. He previously led the Tarrant County Republican Party and also had two unsuccessful state House bids. French did not immediately respond to requests for comment sent to multiple email addresses associated with him.

items.originalTitle: ‘A savagely brutal map’: Senate GOP braces for 2028
items.author: Meredith Lee Hill
items.title: ‘A savagely brutal map’: Senate GOP braces for 2028
items.summary: Sen. Bernie Moreno isn’t sugarcoating things. The incoming chair of the National Republican Senatorial Committee will be in charge of defending 19 GOP seats in 2028 — and he’ll need to flip at least six more to regain control of the Senate majority. “Looking at it right now, it's absolutely a savagely brutal map,” the Ohio Republican said in an interview on Capitol Hill. After a historic midterms shellacking, Moreno is in the hot seat as he looks to navigate his chamber — and the party — through a rebuilding of its brand and its base over next two years. Republicans will likely have just 44 seats heading into 2028. They need to hold onto seats in battleground states like Wisconsin and North Carolina, while trying to flip seats held by Democratic Sens. Mark Kelly in Arizona, John Fetterman in Pennsylvania, Raphael Warnock in Georgia and Catherine Cortez Masto in Nevada. Moreno and his team have interviewed a handful of candidates over the last few days to be the next NRSC executive director, according to four people with direct knowledge of the matter, granted anonymity to discuss private conversations. Republicans expect Chris Grant, a former Moreno and Trump campaign staffer who now runs his own firm, to serve as a main outside GOP consultant for the committee. On top of the grueling map ahead, the Ohio Republican is facing the additional task of working with a lame duck president who still wields immense power over the GOP and its primaries. Then there’s the vice president, who is likely to run for president himself in the same two-year sprint. Moreno is close with both of those men. Asked how involved he expects the White House to be in GOP primaries and recruiting going forward, he replied, “We’re going to work on all of that.” It’ll be a complicated path forward. Moreno, over the past cycle has been unwilling to cast blame on President Donald Trump or Vice President JD Vance. Days before the midterm elections, he said if Republicans lost, it would be because people were “pissed off” about high gas prices. He’s unlikely to completely distance himself and the NRSC brand from the president's influence. But the party is currently undergoing a reckoning of how closely to align with the president after voters delivered an uncompromising rebuke of Trump’s economic agenda. Across the country, several battlegrounds and once-thought-to-be-safe red territory fell to Democratic hands. Trump in the 2026 cycle angered many Senate Republicans by supporting a primary challenge against Sen. John Cornyn of Texas — a move they privately say cost them north of $200 million as they tried, in vain, to save Ken Paxton’s imperiled campaign. The president also supported a primary challenge against Sen. Bill Cassidy of Louisiana, and pushed Sen. Thom Tillis to decide to retire in highly competitive North Carolina. One of the biggest challenges before Moreno and Senate Republicans after the midterms wipeout is to find candidates who can win a general election in highly competitive states, while also making it through GOP primaries where Trump will be a major factor. They’ll need to push back on the White House if the president tries, once again, to intervene — though that’s easier said than done. “There will be no patience for bad recruits this cycle,” said one senior Republican granted anonymity to discuss internal conversations, referring to the implosions of Paxton, Michael Whatley in North Carolina and other Republicans who were hand-picked by Trump. The White House referred POLITICO to Trump's post-midterms comments, where he blamed his party’s losses on the fact that he wasn’t on the ballot and said he brought several candidates "closer to victory," though they ultimately lost. Senate Majority Leader John Thune — who will be the minority leader next year — and his team plan to be heavily involved in recruitment efforts, according to two people involved in the conversations, granted anonymity to speak candidly. Their goal, one of the people said, is “to make sure we have our strongest possible candidates on the ballot in 2028.” Moreno is already trying to find a GOP recruit in his home state of Ohio to run against incoming Democratic Sen. Sherrod Brown, whose term will be up again in 2028 after he won a special election against GOP Sen. Jon Husted earlier this month. The new NRSC chair said he’s looking for “somebody who can beat the crap out of Sherrod Brown.” Husted in private conversations hasn’t completely ruled out another bid, but he’s indicated he’s unlikely to run again, according to three people with knowledge of the matter, granted anonymity to speak candidly. Ohio Republicans expect former state Sen. Kevin Coughlin to explore a potential Senate bid. And they’re watching Rep. Mike Turner (R-Ohio), who just lost his reelection. Husted did not respond to a request for comment. A Turner spokesperson said in a statement that the representative "has been approached by several people about this and is keeping all his options open.” If Vance doesn’t seek his own presidential bid, Republicans in his home state are holding a long-shot hope that he, too, might consider a return to his old job. “JD Vance would be a dream candidate,” said one Ohio Republican.
